title: Anak Krakatau Eruption Sends Ash 50,000 Feet High, Disrupts Thousands of Flights
summary: A powerful eruption at Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano sent ash soaring up to 15,000 meters (50,000 feet) into the atmosphere, disrupting air travel and worsening air quality across parts of the country. The volcano, located between the islands of Java and Sumatra, entered a prolonged explosive phase in early September 2026 that lasted more than 24 hours. Satellites captured the dramatic scene. One image from NASA's Landsat 8 satellite showed a bright white plume of volcanic gas rising above a darker brown cloud of ash. A broader view from the Suomi NPP satellite revealed volcanic material spreading across a much wider area. By September 6, Indonesia's meteorological agency reported ash had climbed to 6,000 meters (20,000 feet) east of the volcano and as high as 15,000 meters (50,000 feet) to the west. The high concentration of ash forced the temporary closure of eight airports across Java and Sumatra. According to news reports, nearly 3,000 flights into and out of the region were disrupted. Ash also fell over populated areas, including Jakarta and other parts of West Java. Volcanic ash can pose health concerns because it may irritate the respiratory system, eyes, and skin. The Indonesian Humanitarian Coordination Platform noted that the hazard differs from smoke produced by peatland fires elsewhere in Indonesia. Volcanic ash and wildfire smoke have different particle properties, travel differently through the atmosphere, and require different protective measures. The volcano's sustained explosive activity weakened on September 6, though Anak Krakatau continued to rumble. Its activity shifted back toward a more typical pattern of Strombolian eruptions—periodic bursts of ash and other volcanic material. Airports had resumed operation by September 8. Even so, Anak Krakatau remained at the second-highest alert level on Indonesia's volcanic warning scale, a status it has held since early July. Scientists continue to monitor the volcano closely, as it is capable of much more hazardous activity.
why_it_matters: The eruption shows how a single geological event can ripple through global systems — aviation, public health, air quality and emergency planning — within days. For a 12-14 year old growing up in a crowded, connected world, it is a case study in why monitoring, early warning and coordinated shutdowns matter, and why living near a volcano is a permanent trade-off between fertile land and recurring risk.

background_read: Anak Krakatau (Indonesian for 'Child of Krakatau') is a young volcanic island that grew out of the caldera left by the catastrophic 1883 eruption of Krakatau. That blast was heard thousands of kilometres away, triggered deadly tsunamis and killed tens of thousands of people, making it one of the most destructive eruptions ever recorded.

Indonesia sits along the Ring of Fire, the belt of volcanic and earthquake zones around the Pacific where most of the world's active volcanoes are found, which is why the country experiences eruptions so often.

Anak Krakatau is dangerous in a second way: when part of its flank collapsed during an eruption in December 2018, the landslide pushed a tsunami into coastal Java and Sumatra that killed more than 400 people. Scientists therefore treat the volcano as a serious hazard, not just a spectacular sight.

Volcanic ash is a serious threat to aviation because it can melt inside hot jet engines and coat turbine blades. After Iceland's Eyjafjallajökull eruption grounded roughly 100,000 flights in 2010, airlines and governments expanded ash advisory systems that now help decide when airspace must close.

Satellites such as NASA's Landsat 8 (an Earth-observing satellite) and Suomi NPP (a US weather satellite) routinely track ash clouds and help forecasters warn aircraft and communities in the ash's path.

perspectives.description: Satellites, the meteorological agency and ash advisory systems detected the plume quickly, airports closed before aircraft flew into danger, and service resumed within days of the activity easing. The distinction officials drew between volcanic ash and peatland fire smoke also helped people use the right protection. This is disaster management functioning largely as designed.

Nearly 3,000 disrupted flights mean stranded passengers, lost business, delayed medical supplies and financial losses for airlines and airports. Ash falling on Jakarta and West Java raises health risks, especially for people with existing lung problems, and poorer communities may lack masks or clean air indoors. Anak Krakatau has held a high alert level for months, leaving residents in a state of chronic uncertainty.

Anak Krakatau has erupted repeatedly since it emerged from the 1883 caldera, and its current behaviour — long explosive phases followed by Strombolian bursts — fits a well-documented cycle. The 2018 flank collapse and tsunami showed that the greatest danger may be the volcano's instability rather than the ash itself, which is why scientists keep it under continuous surveillance.

The next priorities are strengthening ash forecasting, reviewing how quickly airspace should reopen, and improving evacuation plans for coastal communities vulnerable to tsunamis from flank collapse. Better regional cooperation on air traffic and long-term monitoring could reduce both the economic damage and the risk to life in future eruptions.
